name: Threads of Tradition
description:
Learn to adorn by hand, one mirror and one stitch at a time! 
This hands-on workshop introduces the Lambadi tradition of mirror embroidery, an art that transforms fabric into a shimmering record of beauty, heritage, and pride. Participants will learn to attach mirrors to cloth using traditional stitches and motifs, guided directly by artisans of the Porgai Artisans Association from Sittilingi Valley, Tamil Nadu. 
Traditionally practiced by Lambadi women to mark textiles with identity and status, this embroidery has been preserved across generations. The workshop is open to complete beginners and welcomes anyone curious about craft, culture, or new ways to personalize a garment. All materials are provided, and those who wish to embellish a piece of their own are welcome to bring it along.

name: Gombe
description:
This evening brings together three short films, followed by a conversation between filmmakers Hansa Thapliyal and Paromita Vohra. Each film turns an intimate lens on questions of art, choice, and connection. 
The Outside In
25m 03s | 2019 | English, Marathi with English Subtitles
Two dollmakers, working with simple, discarded materials, gently loosen our resistance to empathy. The film collaborates with them and their dolls, blurring the line between what lies outside us and within. 
Kya Hai Ye Samjhauta
9m | 2024 | Hindi with English Subtitles
Born from twelve caseworkers’ recordings across rural Uttar Pradesh, this film uses scraps of cloth, needle and thread, and the timbre of human voices to explore women’s choices in the face of domestic violence. This film looks at the word samjhauta and asks: do you make your terms? 
Duniya Kee Raunak
19m 40s | 2026 | Telugu, Marathi, Hindi with English Subtitles
Must a television screen decide what our lives will be like? Little Mansoor steps beyond his window to befriend the world outside. Blending shadow puppetry, theatre, and stop motion, the film is a tribute to the earliest, most playful histories of cinema. 
Please Note: Children under 16 are to be accompanied by an adult. 
Venue: Seminar Halls

name: The Four Billion Year Old Story of Consciousness
description:
We tend to think of humans as special because of our superior intelligence, a story that runs from spotting poisonous berries to Descartes’ I think, therefore I am, and now, to the machines we worry will out-think us. This conversation asks a different question: was cognition ever really what made us human, or is that just the story intelligence tells about itself? 
The deeper question addressed is not how we came to think, but rather how we came to cooperate. In ancient times, capabilities were shared across a group: one read the stars, another tracked prey. Cognition was distributed, and cooperation was mutually beneficial. This discussion argues that perhaps, intelligence did not come first. Perhaps, consciousness evolved less to help us think, and more to help us stay together.

name: The Many Pasts of Panipat, 1761
description:
A great “what if?” moment in Indian history, the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761 has produced martyrs, ballads, and endless partisan debate. This lecture examines how its retelling, across school textbooks, Hindu nationalist historiography, and cinema, has flattened a complex event into a tale of heroes and villains. It raises the question, whose Panipat are we really remembering? 
The vernacular primary sources tell a different story: where popular memory insists on certainty, they equivocate, contradict, and complicate. A micro history of the battle reveals multiple pasts, remembered and recorded by multiple men. This lecture makes a case for why critical historians cannot ignore this plurality while narrating the event to a generation raised on a communal rendering of Indian history. 
About Satish Chandra 
Professor Satish Chandra (1922-2017) was one of India’s foremost historians and a towering authority on medieval Indian history. Over a distinguished four-decade career, he taught at leading universities across the country, including Allahabad University, Aligarh Muslim University, Delhi University, Rajasthan University, and finally Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU). At JNU, he co-founded the Centre for Historical Studies alongside S. Gopal, Bipin Chandra, and Romila Thapar. As Chairman of the University Grants Commission, he went on to help shape academic life across India, and in 1985, deeply committed to intellectual exchange, he co-founded the Society for Indian Ocean Studies. A thoughtful historian who brought a Marxist approach to the field, Chandra’s work bridged eras and ideas, leaving an enduring mark on the study of India’s past. 
Presented by: 
Alok Chandra

name: Rediscovering Play
description:
This workshop explores India’s traditional games, from seed-sowing board games to lively outdoor play, passed down across generations. Participants will learn and play a curated selection of five to eight games chosen to suit the group, discovering the strategy, wit, and community spirit built into each one. What might a game invented centuries ago still have to teach us about patience, cooperation, and joy? 
The session moves between quiet, tactical play and boisterous group games, layering theory into hands-on practice as participants pick up rules, strategies, and the stories behind them. Games are drawn from a wider repertoire and vary by group, spanning seed-sowing games like Pallankuzhi and Alukuzhi Mane, dice-based games such as Thayam and Pagade, strategy games including the Tower of Brahma and Goat and Tiger, war-strategy games like Country Chess and Nine Men’s Morris, and bonus play with spinning tops, marbles, and cup and ball. No prior experience is necessary. Traditional games are living heritage. As carriers of mathematical logic, social rhythm, and cultural memory, these games continue to reward a room of strangers as readily as a family across three generations.

name: The Resurrection Quest
description:
121 min | English with subtitles | United States, China, Germany, Kenya, Russia, Singapore, UAE 
Blending science with emotional depth, this documentary is a cinematic essay on our relationship with life, death, and the illusions of control. Spanning seven countries, it explores humanity’s audacious pursuit of one of the most radical scientific frontiers of our time: the reversal of extinction. Is de-extinction hubris, or hope? 
From cloning pets and engineering extinct birds to reviving ancient ecosystems, the film offers an intimate, urgent look at the dream of second chances, and its consequences. At the heart of the films lies the concept of Samsara; a cyclical journey through grief, hope, death, and renewal. As species vanish and ecosystems unravel, the film follows scientists and conservationists chasing what was lost, be it a beloved dog, an extinct pigeon, the last northern white rhinos, or even a gene-edited, cold-resistant elephant standing in for the woolly mammoth. But beneath the technology lie harder questions still: who decides which species return, and who gets access to the tools that bring them back?

name: Svara Darshan
description:
This morning concert offers an intimate encounter with the world of Hindustani music. Moving between traditional and contemporary compositions, musicians draw on the rich heritage as it continues to blossom. Older bandish carry the imprint of the musicians who shaped them, while newer compositions reveal a tradition still very much alive, still evolving in real time. 
Through the interplay of raga, laya-taal, and improvisation, the performance traces how a shared musical language keeps discovering new shapes within familiar rules. Together, they invite the audience to listen more closely, to the movement of a raga, the poetry of a bandish, and the fine grain of a svara as it unfolds. This concert will be followed by a Music Appreciation Workshop, extending the listening experience into a closer look at the language and aesthetics of Hindustani music.

name: From Appreciation to Connoisseurship
description:
In a world of constant noise, listening with interest, intent and without interruption is a phenomenal skill. 
This interactive workshop offers a friendly, accessible introduction to Hindustani art music for listeners with little or no prior exposure. Rather than approaching the tradition through rules and terminology alone, the session teaches participants how to listen, through live demonstration, guided listening exercises, and conversation. What actually happens, moment to moment, within a Hindustani performance? 
Participants will pick up some of the tradition’s fundamental concepts and forms, learning to identify the musical elements at work and to appreciate the choices a performer makes in real time. The focus is on building the ear of an engaged, informed listener. No prior musical knowledge is required; simply a passion for learning and an interest in the art.

name: Moksha Mudra
description:
This Bharatanatyam production traces the parallel cycles of women and the earth, each unfolding through the turn of the seasons. As the earth moves through its changing forms, its female protagonists move through their own inner seasons, carrying turmoil that mirrors the natural world around them before dissolving into liberation. 
Through evocative movement, music, and storytelling, the work moves between distinct narratives: the grace of Amrapali, the devotion of Radha, the resilience of Sita, the courage of Rani Lakshmibai, and the environmental legacy of Amrita Devi. Each episode draws out a different facet of feminine strength and transformation, building toward a single, layered portrait of endurance across time.

name: Odyssey
description:
Odyssey explores the human experience through Bharatanatyam, weaving together compositions from various languages and composers, spanning centuries of tradition and feeling. From the carefree days of childhood to the wisdom of age, each of us walks a path shaped by emotion, experience, and meaning. What does it take to simply enjoy the ride? 
Revisiting the joy of childhood and the hope and love of youth, the piece reflects honestly on how expectations, ego, and anxiety can pull us from what truly matters. It also showcases the beautiful moments of the journey too: the moments we let go, open our hearts, and rediscover life’s deeper purpose.

name: Gandhi’s Long Shadow
description:
Gandhi’s ideas did not go unchallenged, even by those closest to his moment in history. This talk draws on the book Arguments with Gandhi, examining the ideological disagreements he had with Marxists, religious fundamentalists, economic modernizers, and anti-caste radicals. What can a century of disagreement teach us about how to live now? 
Using Gandhi’s legacy as a lens, the talk offers a moral and political history of the modern world, one built as much from argument as from agreement. Gandhi’s debates with his contemporaries, and later generations’ arguments with him, foreground questions we have yet to resolve: how do we resist political tyranny? How do we address discrimination based on caste, gender, and race? And how do we achieve freedom from poverty without destroying the planet along the way?
